[[:db/retract 17592186220225 :answer-field/choices 17592186220226] [:db/retract 17592186220225 :answer-field/choices 17592186220227] [:db/retract 17592186220225 :answer-field/choices 17592186220228] [:db/retract 17592186220225 :answer-field/choices 17592186220229] [:db/retract 17592186220225 :answer-field/choices 17592186220230] [:db/retract 17592186220237 :answer-field/choices 17592186220240] [:db/retract 17592186220237 :answer-field/choices 17592186220241] [:db/retract 17592186220237 :answer-field/choices 17592186220242] [:db/retract 17592186220237 :answer-field/choices 17592186220238] [:db/retract 17592186220237 :answer-field/choices 17592186220239] {:db/id 17592186221430 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-056683d5-9c10-553b-93b1-01f7db0cfa24" "question-954d3e87-b1ac-516e-bb73-13e2611b178e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221157 :question/worked-solution "We know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau) \, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t) = \cos(\pi t).$ Thus, for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi τ)\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221431 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a9ec2e0a-7b21-59e9-965b-b9f812cb11e6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221158 :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s) = \frac{1}{s(s-1)} = \frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s) = \dfrac{1}{s-1}.$
Also, we know that

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={e}^{τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221432 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a4855477-bdfa-5214-b5d7-5a97d7d6e1ba" "question-72ddd4c8-8e72-5f66-b964-d1ec00d699bb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221163 :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that $A'(t) = f(t)$ and $A(0) ={ 0}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\dfrac{1}{s}e^{-st} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ we have $-\dfrac{1}{s}A(t)e^{-st}\bigg|_0^{\infty} = {0}$ and

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}A(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
= \dfrac{1}{s}\int_0^{\infty}{ e^{-st} A'(t)} \,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Finally, using that $A'(t) = f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-056683d5-9c10-553b-93b1-01f7db0cfa24" :question/id #uuid "056683d5-9c10-553b-93b1-01f7db0cfa24" :question/math-academy-id "q-330828" :question/problem "Given that $L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}$ for $s>a$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{(3/4)τ}\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>\frac{3}{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "We know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)={e}^{(3/4)t}.$ Thus, for $s>\frac{3}{4},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{(3/4)t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{3}{4})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>\frac{3}{4},$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{(3/4)τ}\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s(s-\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{4}{s(4s-3)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1c3a0a01-7462-57a7-ba8f-e0b8d49c956f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1c3a0a01-7462-57a7-ba8f-e0b8d49c956f" :answer-field/id #uuid "1c3a0a01-7462-57a7-ba8f-e0b8d49c956f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3c3d659d-d6ec-5e9b-87ec-2f606fd5411d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b0fcf8bd-187b-515e-98be-9d23bc084284" "answer-20e282f4-88ec-52d6-8ea7-9a6576df4b1f" "answer-344220eb-e137-5ef4-9290-8367a1f2b18c" "answer-07d7257d-8558-5174-b584-bebeccdc3e51" "answer-3c3d659d-d6ec-5e9b-87ec-2f606fd5411d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b0fcf8bd-187b-515e-98be-9d23bc084284" :answer/id #uuid "b0fcf8bd-187b-515e-98be-9d23bc084284" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4s-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-20e282f4-88ec-52d6-8ea7-9a6576df4b1f" :answer/id #uuid "20e282f4-88ec-52d6-8ea7-9a6576df4b1f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4s-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-344220eb-e137-5ef4-9290-8367a1f2b18c" :answer/id #uuid "344220eb-e137-5ef4-9290-8367a1f2b18c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-07d7257d-8558-5174-b584-bebeccdc3e51" :answer/id #uuid "07d7257d-8558-5174-b584-bebeccdc3e51" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{4s-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3c3d659d-d6ec-5e9b-87ec-2f606fd5411d" :answer/id #uuid "3c3d659d-d6ec-5e9b-87ec-2f606fd5411d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{s(4s-3)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-954d3e87-b1ac-516e-bb73-13e2611b178e" :question/id #uuid "954d3e87-b1ac-516e-bb73-13e2611b178e" :question/math-academy-id "q-330821" :question/problem "Given that $L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}$ for $s>a$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{3τ}\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>3.$" :question/worked-solution "We know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)={e}^{3t}.$ Thus, for $s>3,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>3,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{3τ}\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s(s-3)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-61080eee-c12c-5456-b01c-6b7bdcb3d31a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-61080eee-c12c-5456-b01c-6b7bdcb3d31a" :answer-field/id #uuid "61080eee-c12c-5456-b01c-6b7bdcb3d31a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8616a0a9-5e4c-5a5b-b120-d0f5a87babe9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8616a0a9-5e4c-5a5b-b120-d0f5a87babe9" "answer-ca93bd69-e78e-5e89-9ce8-c601d0049523" "answer-65f194c1-4a31-5dc6-9dd1-b74fb4074cce" "answer-e50db842-81cd-53f3-991f-23b6b0d1af22" "answer-f7e331c7-00aa-5a0a-a9ad-b24650546570"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8616a0a9-5e4c-5a5b-b120-d0f5a87babe9" :answer/id #uuid "8616a0a9-5e4c-5a5b-b120-d0f5a87babe9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{s(s-3)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ca93bd69-e78e-5e89-9ce8-c601d0049523" :answer/id #uuid "ca93bd69-e78e-5e89-9ce8-c601d0049523" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{s-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-65f194c1-4a31-5dc6-9dd1-b74fb4074cce" :answer/id #uuid "65f194c1-4a31-5dc6-9dd1-b74fb4074cce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{s-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e50db842-81cd-53f3-991f-23b6b0d1af22" :answer/id #uuid "e50db842-81cd-53f3-991f-23b6b0d1af22" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f7e331c7-00aa-5a0a-a9ad-b24650546570" :answer/id #uuid "f7e331c7-00aa-5a0a-a9ad-b24650546570" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{s}{s-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186304855 :question/problem "Given that $L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2τ)\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>0.$" :question/worked-solution "We know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$ Thus, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2τ)\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221938 :question/problem "Given that $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{2}\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>0.$" :question/worked-solution "We know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)={t}^{2}.$ Thus, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{t}^{2}\} \\  & =\frac{2!}{{s}^{2+1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{2}\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186220225 :answer-field/correct "answer-4b585c91-a64d-5156-9b47-3ab3be96c10e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a12e3278-78eb-5071-8f80-02016ffa5453" "answer-7393820c-ee1c-5fad-afb6-cfabaf3f9ba5" "answer-4b585c91-a64d-5156-9b47-3ab3be96c10e" "answer-31bff94b-20f3-5f6b-a517-e5ef54908756" "answer-d12a242e-7964-5cb0-85a3-8ccfe0400402"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a12e3278-78eb-5071-8f80-02016ffa5453" :answer/id #uuid "a12e3278-78eb-5071-8f80-02016ffa5453" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{{s}^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7393820c-ee1c-5fad-afb6-cfabaf3f9ba5" :answer/id #uuid "7393820c-ee1c-5fad-afb6-cfabaf3f9ba5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b585c91-a64d-5156-9b47-3ab3be96c10e" :answer/id #uuid "4b585c91-a64d-5156-9b47-3ab3be96c10e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{{s}^{4}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-31bff94b-20f3-5f6b-a517-e5ef54908756" :answer/id #uuid "31bff94b-20f3-5f6b-a517-e5ef54908756" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{{s}^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d12a242e-7964-5cb0-85a3-8ccfe0400402" :answer/id #uuid "d12a242e-7964-5cb0-85a3-8ccfe0400402" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186304853 :question/problem "Given that $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>0.$" :question/worked-solution "We know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)={t}^{3}.$ Thus, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{t}^{3}\} \\  & =\frac{3!}{{s}^{3+1}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a9ec2e0a-7b21-59e9-965b-b9f812cb11e6" :question/id #uuid "a9ec2e0a-7b21-59e9-965b-b9f812cb11e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-330846" :question/problem "For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-4)},\,s>4
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a},\text{ }s>a.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-4)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-4}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\} \\  & ={e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{4τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({e}^{4t}-1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-998aa03e-483d-5aca-ad28-ce026cba4873"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-998aa03e-483d-5aca-ad28-ce026cba4873" :answer-field/id #uuid "998aa03e-483d-5aca-ad28-ce026cba4873" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-27a1e96a-2d02-5798-a435-19834cb6e962" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3a067135-e5b7-55d1-925b-a9eb022c03a2" "answer-27a1e96a-2d02-5798-a435-19834cb6e962" "answer-27216b69-d2aa-588b-b25c-49b94f88c580" "answer-bdf7be69-473e-55c0-88f8-9515389c2337" "answer-eaa42c98-56c6-5b90-8cdd-cf61b5f56f21"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3a067135-e5b7-55d1-925b-a9eb022c03a2" :answer/id #uuid "3a067135-e5b7-55d1-925b-a9eb022c03a2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(1-{e}^{4t})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-27a1e96a-2d02-5798-a435-19834cb6e962" :answer/id #uuid "27a1e96a-2d02-5798-a435-19834cb6e962" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}({e}^{4t}-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-27216b69-d2aa-588b-b25c-49b94f88c580" :answer/id #uuid "27216b69-d2aa-588b-b25c-49b94f88c580" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}({e}^{t}-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bdf7be69-473e-55c0-88f8-9515389c2337" :answer/id #uuid "bdf7be69-473e-55c0-88f8-9515389c2337" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{t-4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eaa42c98-56c6-5b90-8cdd-cf61b5f56f21" :answer/id #uuid "eaa42c98-56c6-5b90-8cdd-cf61b5f56f21" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{4t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221940 :question/problem "For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{2}{{s}^{4}},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{2}{{s}^{4}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2!}{{s}^{2+1}}\} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{2}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}

Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & ={{field-4}}(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & ={{field-6}}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}

$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}

[:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222478 :tutorial/content "Suppose a quantity increases over time at a rate proportional to its current value, such as the balance of a bank account growing with continuous interest. The Laplace transform can be used to analyze how such exponential growth behaves, especially when the function is **integrated over time** to represent total accumulation.

To illustrate this, we’ll find the Laplace transform of a function defined as the integral of an exponential function. This shows how *integration in the time domain* corresponds to *division by $s$* in the $s$-domain.

Suppose we are given that 

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s>a.
$$

Let's find the Laplace transform of

$$
g(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau/2}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad s > \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

We apply the **Integration in Time Property**: if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\!\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=e^{t/2}$. Thus, for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{t/2}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\,\{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ/2}\,dτ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s\,(s-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{s(2s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221464 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi τ)\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221431 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a9ec2e0a-7b21-59e9-965b-b9f812cb11e6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221158 :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$

$$

where $F(s) = \dfrac{1}{s-1}.$
Also, we know that

$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}

Additionally, we know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={e}^{τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221432 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a4855477-bdfa-5214-b5d7-5a97d7d6e1ba" "question-72ddd4c8-8e72-5f66-b964-d1ec00d699bb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221163 :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that $A'(t) = f(t)$ and $A(0) ={ 0}.$ Then,

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-056683d5-9c10-553b-93b1-01f7db0cfa24" :question/id #uuid "056683d5-9c10-553b-93b1-01f7db0cfa24" :question/math-academy-id "q-330828" :question/problem "Given that $L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}$ for $s>a$, find the Laplace transform of

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186302374 :question/problem "For the function

$L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186304856 :question/problem "For the function

Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & ={{field-4}}(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & ={{field-6}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ=A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{{{field-2}}\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={{field-3}} \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)({{field-4}}){|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & ={{field-6}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5170c363-4e67-51f6-b130-fd0a17a1796b" "answer-field-6da3b0d3-6b5c-5e60-962c-307a26bf1c26" [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186222478 :tutorial/content "Suppose a quantity increases over time at a rate proportional to its current value, such as the balance of a bank account growing with continuous interest. The Laplace transform can be used to analyze how such exponential growth behaves, especially when the function is **integrated over time** to represent total accumulation.

To illustrate this, we’ll find the Laplace transform of a function defined as the integral of an exponential function. This shows how *integration in the time domain* corresponds to *division by $s$* in the $s$-domain.

Suppose we are given that 

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s>a.
$$

Let's find the Laplace transform of

$$
g(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau/2}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad s > \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

We apply the **Integration in Time Property**: if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\!\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=e^{t/2}$. Thus, for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{t/2}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\,\{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ/2}\,dτ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s\,(s-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{s(2s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221464 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186221157 :question/worked-solution "We know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau) \, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t) = \cos(\pi t).$ Thus, for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi τ)\,\text{d}τ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186221158 :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s) = \frac{1}{s(s-1)} = \frac{F(s)}{s},

Also, we know that

$$

$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={e}^{τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}-1.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186221163 :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that $A'(t) = f(t)$ and $A(0) ={ 0}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\dfrac{1}{s}e^{-st} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ we have $-\dfrac{1}{s}A(t)e^{-st}\bigg|_0^{\infty} = {0}$ and

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}A(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
= \dfrac{1}{s}\int_0^{\infty}{ e^{-st} A'(t)} \,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Finally, using that $A'(t) = f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}

$$"] ["question-a4855477-bdfa-5214-b5d7-5a97d7d6e1ba" :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$

}_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=$  {{field-1}}. Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ=A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{{{field-2}}\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={{field-3}} \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)({{field-4}}){|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & ={{field-6}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-72ddd4c8-8e72-5f66-b964-d1ec00d699bb" :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-72ddd4c8-8e72-5f66-b964-d1ec00d699bb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5170c363-4e67-51f6-b130-fd0a17a1796b" :answer-field/id #uuid :knowledge-point/questions "question-72ddd4c8-8e72-5f66-b964-d1ec00d699bb"] [17592186222478 :tutorial/content "Suppose a quantity increases over time at a rate proportional to its current value, such as the balance of a bank account growing with continuous interest. The Laplace transform can be used to analyze how such exponential growth behaves, especially when the function is **integrated over time** to represent total accumulation.

To illustrate this, we’ll find the Laplace transform of a function defined as the integral of an exponential function. This shows how *integration in the time domain* corresponds to *division by $s$* in the $s$-domain.

Suppose we are given that 

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s>a.
$$

Let's find the Laplace transform of

$$
g(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau/2}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad s > \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

We apply the **Integration in Time Property**: if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\!\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=e^{t/2}$. Thus, for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{t/2}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\,\{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ/2}\,dτ\} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s\,(s-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{s(2s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186221464 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0]] "retractions" [[17592186221157 :question/worked-solution "We know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

= \dfrac{1}{s}\int_0^{\infty}{ e^{-st} A'(t)} \,\mathrm{d}t.

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186222478 :tutorial/content "Suppose a quantity increases over time at a rate proportional to its current value, such as the balance of a bank account growing with continuous interest. The Laplace transform can be used to analyze how such exponential growth behaves, especially when the function is **integrated over time** to represent total accumulation.

To illustrate this, we’ll find the Laplace transform of a function defined as the integral of an exponential function. This shows how *integration in the time domain* corresponds to *division by $s$* in the $s$-domain.

Suppose we are given that 

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s>a.
$$

Let's find the Laplace transform of

$$
g(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau/2}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad s > \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

We apply the **Integration in Time Property**: if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\!\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=e^{t/2}$. Thus, for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{{e}^{t/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L\,{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ/2}\,dτ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s\,(s-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{s(2s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$"]]}

$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={e}^{τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}-1.\end{aligned}

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2})},\,s>0

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2})}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{L}^{-1}{\frac{\pi }{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{\pi }\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & =-\frac{1}{{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{{\pi }^{2}}\,(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186304856 :question/id #uuid "409ed1af-a518-5652-a26f-cb341eaa1c80" :question/math-academy-id "q-330838" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186221431 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a65eeb21-bcd5-542d-8277-04dab7fa9b53" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Inverse Laplace Transform Using the Integral Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03a3c959-75ca-5441-bcf3-23d4f787222c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))" :db/id 17592186302479} {:answer/id #uuid "1bef64cc-0d2c-5f98-a507-02d1052185e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)" :db/id 17592186302638} {:answer/id #uuid "71add469-2d90-55dc-be03-2e3a39950b8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))" :db/id 17592186303145} {:answer/id #uuid "8487079f-256c-548b-9b50-71e2a3f7c818" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))" :db/id 17592186303282} {:answer/id #uuid "b14358a0-e002-52d4-aaa1-35404f1569bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))" :db/id 17592186303549}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "71add469-2d90-55dc-be03-2e3a39950b8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))" :db/id 17592186303145} :answer-field/id #uuid "36d309ae-5289-56fe-8e78-f5864b8353f7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186304219}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "For the function

$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186304857 :question/id #uuid "c43f625b-d110-5aef-9243-2a1cae536c09" :question/math-academy-id "q-330843"} {:db/id 17592186304858 :question/id #uuid "37553079-b450-5c8e-9348-e4ed61dd6d77" :question/math-academy-id "q-330845" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186221431 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a65eeb21-bcd5-542d-8277-04dab7fa9b53" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Inverse Laplace Transform Using the Integral Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f80b316-6731-5f5a-9dec-739fd3be6c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{720}{{t}^{7}}" :db/id 17592186302559} {:answer/id #uuid "25d0f0bf-2b54-519f-94e7-adf5da66e6c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{t}^{6}" :db/id 17592186302700} {:answer/id #uuid "42d5d705-b17e-599c-8fd8-42db38dbf6ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{8}}{56}" :db/id 17592186302880} {:answer/id #uuid "902b0ead-51de-5d7b-bd8f-d5add3c46114" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}" :db/id 17592186303356} {:answer/id #uuid "b6cdff7d-b0fc-5867-b70b-88bd55c14f14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}" :db/id 17592186303589}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b6cdff7d-b0fc-5867-b70b-88bd55c14f14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}" :db/id 17592186303589} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e69e93c-a037-567a-be3b-ba40f212fcb1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186304418}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the function

$$

$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that

$$
G(s)=\frac{720}{{s}^{8}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},

where $F(s)=\frac{720}{{s}^{7}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{720}{{s}^{7}}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{6!}{{s}^{6+1}}} \\  & ={t}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{6}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186304859 :question/id #uuid "8064a487-d480-5cc5-97a5-d474531a9775" :question/math-academy-id "q-330849"} {:db/id 17592186370079 :question/id #uuid "55ba2de5-4728-586d-af2e-e9e7120ebc2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-330842"} {:db/id 17592186370086 :question/id #uuid "edb23ffa-161e-5239-9f82-d504d4a4ac87" :question/math-academy-id "q-330850"} {:db/id 17592186370093 :question/id #uuid "5f444b78-bec6-52bd-a9f4-914af7fbf539" :question/math-academy-id "q-330853"} {:db/id 17592186221432 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221163 :question/id #uuid "602b037e-28bf-5afd-a466-652668bf08c6" :question/math-academy-id "e-21551"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "51dfecdb-ad66-5e07-8873-ca8e116b27bd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049543} {:db/id 17592186050929}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221936 :question/id #uuid "4e170618-c144-579d-a704-aa29df6a71b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-329472"} {:db/id 17592186221944 :question/id #uuid "ba1d32c7-91d0-5ea9-ae96-737c7cf8e6a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-331052"} {:db/id 17592186304886 :question/id #uuid "32d46b6e-c28b-5a1b-acb4-7332fefea078" :question/math-academy-id "q-331084"} {:db/id 17592186370100 :question/id #uuid "c7ba6935-6849-517e-9bd9-9735ae2d6fb9" :question/math-academy-id "q-331076"}] :knowledge-point/title "Proving the Formula for Laplace Transforms of Integrals"} {:db/id 17592186221163 :question/id #uuid "602b037e-28bf-5afd-a466-652668bf08c6" :question/math-academy-id "e-21551" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186221432 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "51dfecdb-ad66-5e07-8873-ca8e116b27bd" :knowledge-point/title "Proving the Formula for Laplace Transforms of Integrals"}] :question/problem "Prove that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\, d\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that $A'(t) = f(t)$ and $A(0) ={ 0}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\dfrac{1}{s}e^{-st} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ we have $-\dfrac{1}{s}A(t)e^{-st}\bigg|_0^{\infty} = {0}$ and

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}A(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
= \dfrac{1}{s}\int_0^{\infty}{ e^{-st} A'(t)} \,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Finally, using that $A'(t) = f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049543} {:db/id 17592186050929} {:db/id 17592186221936 :question/id #uuid "4e170618-c144-579d-a704-aa29df6a71b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-329472"} {:db/id 17592186221944 :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222352 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222478 :tutorial/content "Suppose a quantity increases over time at a rate proportional to its current value, such as the balance of a bank account growing with continuous interest. The Laplace transform can be used to analyze how such exponential growth behaves, especially when the function is **integrated over time** to represent total accumulation.

To illustrate this, we’ll find the Laplace transform of a function defined as the integral of an exponential function. This shows how *integration in the time domain* corresponds to *division by $s$* in the $s$-domain.

Suppose we are given that 

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s>a.
$$

Let's find the Laplace transform of

$$
g(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau/2}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad s > \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

We apply the **Integration in Time Property**: if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\!\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=e^{t/2}$. Thus, for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{{e}^{t/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L\,{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ/2}\,dτ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s\,(s-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{s(2s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ee57f084-2127-562e-bf7b-91641db97ba1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14359 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e6f15f22-f7c7-5bf4-a482-3a5056a94c4b" :step/math-academy-id 599887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222353}} {:db/id 17592186222353 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222525 :tutorial/content "Assume that

- $f(t)$ is *piecewise continuous* on $[0,\infty)$, and

- $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a$.

Then the Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=\mathcal L\{f(t)\}
$$

exists for all $s>a$, and we have the **Integration Property**:

$$
\mathcal L\!\left\{\int_0^t f(\tau)\,\textrm{d}\tau\right\}
= \frac{F(s)}{s},
\qquad s>a.
$$

This result shows that *integrating a function with respect to time* corresponds to *dividing its Laplace transform by $s$*.  

This result allows us to handle accumulated quantities without re-integrating from scratch.

Next, we will apply this property to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "05dac555-11de-5a37-a12e-e9c6ad069388" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14729 :tutorial/title "The General Result"} :step/id #uuid To illustrate this, we’ll find the Laplace transform of a function defined as the integral of an exponential function. This shows how *integration in the time domain* corresponds to *division by $s$* in the $s$-domain.

Suppose we are given that 

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-a}, \qquad s>a.
$$

Let's find the Laplace transform of

$$
g(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau/2}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad s > \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

We apply the **Integration in Time Property**: if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\!\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=e^{t/2}$. Thus, for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{{e}^{t/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L\,{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{τ/2}\,dτ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s\,(s-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{s(2s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ee57f084-2127-562e-bf7b-91641db97ba1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14359 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e6f15f22-f7c7-5bf4-a482-3a5056a94c4b" :step/math-academy-id 599887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222353}} {:db/id 17592186222478 :tutorial/content "Suppose a quantity increases over time at a rate proportional to its current value, such as the balance of a bank account growing with continuous interest. "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in statistical physics and experimental analysis." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1012 155 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1013 "PS2" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1014 #uuid
